sum: Super Micro Computer shares climbed 5.2% on Thursday, riding a broader rebound in AI-related equities as Nvidia and other data-center suppliers recovered from a sharp stretch of losses, according to AP. The advance puts the server maker back in favor alongside the rest of the AI infrastructure complex — though the session's real news came from the analyst desk and the balance sheet rather than the tape.

Raymond James raised its price target on the stock to $65 from $48 on Wednesday while keeping an "Outperform" rating, according to media reports. The upgrade lands as investors weigh a business that is growing fast on paper but still burning cash in its operations.

On the product front, Super Micro unveiled a joint KV-cache storage solution with IBM and NVIDIA on Wednesday. The system pairs Supermicro Petascale all-flash servers with IBM Storage Scale and NVIDIA's Dynamo and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking.

Company testing showed the setup delivering up to 56 times faster time-to-first-token on inputs of 130,000 tokens. That is a concrete performance claim, though its value to investors depends on whether the gains hold up under real customer workloads rather than lab conditions. The broader point is that AI infrastructure is increasingly a stack play — servers, storage, software and networking bundled together — and Super Micro is positioning itself at the center of that bundle.

The same day brought a second partnership: Smartbird announced a collaboration with Super Micro to deliver managed AI infrastructure, part of Smartbird's push to expand its enterprise AI partner network.

Super Micro's fiscal first-quarter 2027 results, released Wednesday, showed revenue of $19.95 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.81 per share — both ahead of analyst expectations. The company also guided fiscal second-quarter revenue to a range of $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion, a forecast rather than a reported figure.

The headline numbers carry a wrinkle. Net income came in at $1.594 billion, yet operating cash flow was negative $434 million. That gap between reported profit and cash generation is the metric worth watching: the revenue level is impressive only if the business can convert it into sustainable margins and better cash conversion.

sum: With a long history of controversy, Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) is one of the most divisive stocks in the market. The company has been growing revenue quickly and remains a clear beneficiary of the AI build-out. However, it also has a history of accounting issues, and three now-former employees have been charged by the Department of Justice with violating U.S. technology export bans. As such, the stock is down by more than 35% over the past year, while rivals Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise have more than doubled over the same period.

Supermicro designs and assembles servers and rack solutions for data centers. It normally customizes its systems around Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), and provides turnkey solutions that include things like networking, cooling, and software. The company has said its big advantage is speed, as its integrated rack solutions get customers up and running more quickly.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Despite being a key player in the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, Supermicro has dealt with a lot of issues over the past few years. A short-seller accused the company of accounting irregularities in 2024, and the subsequent investigations eventually led to the company's auditor resigning and delays in its regulatory filings. This was preceded by the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) fining the company in 2020 for improperly recognizing revenue, and in 2018, the stock was delisted from the Nasdaq after the company failed to file financial reports. It did not relist on the exchange until 2020.

The biggest issue the company faces currently, however, is that three former employees, including one of its co-founders, have been charged with illegally smuggling high-end Nvidia GPUs into China through an elaborate scheme that involved fake paperwork, "dummy" servers, and a Thailand-based company that acted as an intermediary. Throughout all these scandals, somehow, CEO Charles Liang has managed to stay in charge.

sum: Intel's blunt warning about memory shortages sent shockwaves through four major hardware makers today, but one of those companies is sitting on a $95 billion AI backlog that could either cushion the blow or make the selloff look like a…

A warning from Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction) that memory shortages are choking PC demand is rippling through the companies that build computers and servers. Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) stock is at $421.74 in afternoon trading, down 11% from its prior close of $475.51. That decline hits a company whose AI server business has been one of the market’s strongest growth stories.

Dell stock is still up 239% year to date (YTD), so some of the selling looks like profit taking after a huge run. Three other hardware makers are decline alongside Dell. Fewer PCs sold means less revenue, while tighter memory supply raises component costs and can cap how many machines a company is able to ship.

Intel laid out the problem on its earnings call on October 29. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said, “In recent weeks, our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability.” He also noted, “Our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell-through.” Tan stated Intel expects the environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize, which reads directly through to Dell and its rivals.

Brian Sozzi of Yahoo Finance argued the broader tech rout is due more to hyperscalers’ ballooning AI spending bills. Sozzi pointed to Google, whose quarterly free cash flow came in at negative $9.1 billion. Amazon posted trailing 12-month free cash flow of negative $42.4 billion. That leaves Dell squeezed from two sides: a weaker PC market and doubts about how long data center spending can last.

HP Inc. (NYSE:HPQ) stock is at $28.99, down 9%, the closest match to Dell’s drop. With Personal Systems making up most of its revenue, the company is the most PC-exposed name in the group. On August 26, HP reported that its total PC unit shipments fell 16% and cited rising memory and storage costs as a risk. Despite trailing its competitors on October 28, HP stock is still up 35% YTD.

sum: Super Micro Computer SMCI and Fabrinet FN are two prominent AI value chain suppliers benefiting from the expansion of AI infrastructure, but they occupy different parts of the supply chain. While Super Micro Computer offers a broad portfolio of rack-scale Total IT Solutions, including complete servers, storage systems, blade servers, subsystems and server management software, Fabrinet provides advanced optical packaging and precision optical, electro-mechanical and electronic manufacturing services to original equipment manufacturers.

With the AI industry growing, both stocks are set to benefit. So the question remains: Which stock has more upside potential? Let’s break down their fundamentals, growth prospects, market challenges and valuation to determine which offers a more compelling investment case.

Super Micro Computer remains positioned to benefit from expanding AI infrastructure demand, supported by rapid adoption of new GPU platforms, its modular Building Block architecture, liquid-cooling expertise and a broader Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) offering. In fourth-quarter fiscal 2026, the company was shipping volume products across NVIDIA’s GB300 NVL72, HGX B300, B200 NVL4 and RTX 6000 Pro lines.

It is also preparing systems based on NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Vera CPU platforms.
